prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- Christine Beatty, chief of staff for former Detroit Mayor Kwame Kilpatrick, pleaded guilty Monday to charges stemming from their text-messaging sex scandal case and will serve four months in jail, according to the Wayne County prosecutor's office. Under a plea deal, Christine Beatty, shown in August at an arraignment in Detroit, will serve five years probation. Beatty pleaded guilty to two counts of obstruction of justice, according to Maria Miller, the prosecutor's spokeswoman. Charges of perjury and misconduct against Beatty will be dropped as part of the plea arrangement, she said. Beatty agreed to a plea arrangement under which she will serve five years probation -- the first 120 days to be served in jail -- and pay a $100,000 fine, "based on [Beatty's] ability to pay," Miller said. Beatty will begin serving her jail sentence on January 5, when she will be formally sentenced, Miller said. Kym L. Worthy, prosecuting attorney for Wayne County, released a statement saying she is "very pleased that this defendant admitted her guilt." "We live in an age where greed and protecting one's secrets is glorified and accepted," Worthy said. "Now the city of Detroit, the region and the state of Michigan can truly begin to move forward when this ugly chapter in Detroit's history is put to rest." In September, Kilpatrick resigned as mayor and pleaded guilty to two felony obstruction of justice charges stemming from his efforts to cover up his relationship with Beatty. Like Beatty, Kilpatrick was sentenced to five years probation with the first four months to be served in jail. He is serving that sentence in the Wayne County jail. At the time of his sentencing in October, the judge in the case called Kilpatrick "arrogant and defiant," particularly for a televised speech that aired hours after Kilpatrick entered his pleas. "That night, the community expected to hear a message of humility, remorse and apology," Wayne County Circuit Judge David Groner said at Kilpatrick's sentencing. "Instead, we heard an arrogant and defiant man who accused the governor, among others, for his downfall." In addition to his jail and probation sentence, Kilpatrick must also pay the city of Detroit $1 million in restitution, and forfeit any future pension. Initially, Kilpatrick was accused of blocking a criminal investigation into his office and firing a police deputy to cover up an affair with Beatty, then his chief of staff. When that deputy, Gary Brown, filed a whistle-blower suit, Kilpatrick and Beatty denied under oath that an affair had taken place between them. Text messages that contradicted Kilpatrick's and Beatty's denials of an affair were made public in January by the Detroit Free Press, and county prosecutor Worthy charged Kilpatrick and Beatty with multiple counts of perjury, obstruction of justice and misconduct in office. The most serious charges would have carried a maximum penalty of 15 years in prison upon conviction. Beatty resigned her post after the text messages were made public. Kilpatrick initially refused to resign after the scandal broke, and Michigan Gov. Jennifer Granholm called a hearing on whether she should remove him from office at the request of the Detroit City Council. Granholm adjourned those hearings after Kilpatrick pleaded guilty and resigned in September.

# Former Detroit aide Christine Beatty pleads guilty in text-message scandal

**DETROIT, Michigan (CNN)** — Christine Beatty, the former chief of staff to Detroit Mayor Kwame Kilpatrick, pleaded guilty Monday to two felony obstruction-of-justice charges stemming from testimony about her relationship with the former mayor.

Beatty admitted that she lied under oath during a 2007 police whistleblower trial when she denied having a romantic relationship with Kilpatrick. Thousands of text messages later made public showed intimate exchanges between the two and appeared to contradict their testimony.

The messages also became central to allegations that Kilpatrick and Beatty misled jurors about the removal of a police official who was investigating misconduct within the mayor’s administration.

Beatty entered the plea as part of an agreement with prosecutors that resolved the criminal case against her. She had initially faced multiple charges, including perjury, obstruction of justice and misconduct in office.

The scandal erupted after the *Detroit Free Press* published excerpts from text messages sent on city-issued pagers. The revelations triggered a criminal investigation and intensified calls for Kilpatrick’s resignation.

Kilpatrick stepped down as mayor in September 2008 after pleading guilty to obstruction of justice and no contest to assaulting or obstructing a police officer. He was sentenced to jail, ordered to pay restitution and barred from holding public office for several years.

Beatty, once one of Kilpatrick’s closest advisers, resigned from her City Hall position as the controversy widened. Her guilty plea marked another major development in a scandal that consumed Detroit’s government and cost the city millions of dollars in legal settlements.

She was scheduled to be sentenced later.

The charges grew out of a whistleblower lawsuit filed by Detroit police officers who said they had been retaliated against while investigating Kilpatrick’s security detail and allegations that Kilpatrick and Beatty were having an affair. Both denied the affair under oath during the 2007 civil trial.

Detroit later agreed to an **$8.4 million settlement** with the officers. Subsequently disclosed text messages between Kilpatrick and Beatty contradicted their sworn testimony and indicated that they had discussed the removal of one of the officers.

He also entered a no-contest plea in a separate case involving an alleged assault on law-enforcement officers. # Former Detroit Official Christine Beatty Sentenced to 120 Days in Text-Message Scandal

**DETROIT —** Christine Beatty, the former chief of staff to ex-Detroit Mayor Kwame Kilpatrick, was sentenced Monday to 120 days in jail for obstructing justice in the text-message scandal that exposed their affair, undermined sworn testimony and helped bring down Kilpatrick’s administration.

Wayne County Circuit Judge Timothy Kenny also placed Beatty on five years’ probation and ordered her to pay $100,000 in restitution to the city. The sentence followed Beatty’s guilty plea to two felony obstruction-of-justice counts. Other charges against her were dismissed under the plea agreement.

The punishment closes the central criminal case against Beatty, once one of the most powerful officials in Detroit government. Prosecutors said she and Kilpatrick lied under oath during a 2007 police whistleblower trial when they denied having a romantic relationship and gave misleading testimony about the removal of a police official.

Beatty apologized before she was sentenced, acknowledging that her conduct had damaged her family, the city and the public’s trust. Kenny nevertheless concluded that incarceration was warranted because the wrongdoing involved sworn testimony by a high-ranking public official.

## Messages contradicted testimony

The scandal began with a lawsuit filed by former Detroit police officers who alleged that they had been punished or forced out after becoming involved in investigations that could embarrass the mayor’s administration.

During the 2007 trial, Kilpatrick and Beatty were questioned under oath about whether they had been romantically involved. Both denied an affair. They also testified about the circumstances surrounding the dismissal of Deputy Police Chief Gary Brown, who claimed he was retaliated against after pursuing an internal investigation.

A jury ruled for the officers, and Detroit eventually agreed to an $8.4 million settlement.

The controversy erupted publicly in January 2008, when the *Detroit Free Press* reported on sexually explicit text messages exchanged between Kilpatrick and Beatty on city-issued pagers. The messages indicated that the two had been intimate and appeared to conflict directly with portions of their trial testimony.

Other messages suggested that Kilpatrick and Beatty had discussed personnel decisions and the handling of the police controversy. The disclosures raised questions not only about perjury, but also about whether city officials had agreed to the multimillion-dollar settlement in an effort to keep the messages from becoming public.

Beatty resigned as chief of staff shortly after the messages were published.

## Criminal charges followed

In March 2008, Wayne County Prosecutor Kym Worthy announced felony charges against both Kilpatrick and Beatty, saying public officials could not be permitted to lie under oath without consequences.

The charges included perjury, obstruction of justice and misconduct in office. Prosecutors alleged that the pair had concealed their relationship and provided false testimony in a case that ultimately cost Detroit millions of dollars.

Kilpatrick resisted calls to resign for months, but his political position deteriorated as the criminal case expanded and additional confrontations with investigators generated new legal problems.

In September 2008, Kilpatrick pleaded guilty to two obstruction-of-justice charges and agreed to step down as mayor. He was sentenced to 120 days in jail, placed on probation and ordered to pay $1 million in restitution to the city. He also agreed to surrender his law license and not seek public office during his probation.

Beatty reached her own plea agreement in December. By admitting to obstruction of justice, she avoided trial on the full set of felony charges but faced the possibility of incarceration.

## A collapse at the top of City Hall

Beatty’s sentencing marks another decisive chapter in a scandal that consumed Detroit government for most of 2008.

What began as an employment dispute inside the Police Department grew into a public corruption crisis after the discovery of electronic messages that contradicted testimony from the mayor and his closest aide. The resulting investigation exposed efforts to conceal information, triggered criminal prosecutions and forced Kilpatrick from office.

For Beatty, the case ends with a felony record, jail time and years of court supervision. For Detroit, it leaves a costly legacy: an $8.4 million civil settlement, additional restitution orders and a prolonged loss of confidence in City Hall.

The scandal’s central issue was ultimately broader than the affair itself. Prosecutors emphasized that the criminal conduct arose from lying under oath and obstructing the judicial process—actions made more serious, they argued, because they were committed by officials entrusted with running the city.
